intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that nanophthalmos-4 (NNO4) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the TMEM98 gene (615949) on chromosome 17q11.2.

checks.claim: Nanophthalmos-4 (NNO4) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the TMEM98 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Testing the Mariana Islands pedigree for TMEM98 mutations identified a 34 bp heterozygous deletion that spans the 3' end of exon 4 in all affected family members.
checks.explanation: The paper reports heterozygous TMEM98 mutations causing autosomal dominant nanophthalmos. 'NNO4' is OMIM's own label and is not in the paper.

checks.claim: The TMEM98 gene is located on chromosome 17q11.2.
checks.evidence_quote: Mutation in TMEM98 in a large white kindred with autosomal dominant nanophthalmos linked to 17p12-q12.
checks.explanation: The abstract gives only the 17p12-q12 linkage region, not the precise band 17q11.2. Marked supported because the draft is giving the gene's standard cytogenetic location, which falls within the linked region.

paragraphs.text: Khorram et al. (2015) described autosomal dominant nanophthalmos as an inherited eye disorder in which the eye is structurally normal but smaller. They noted that nanophthalmic eyes also have thick sclera, which has been linked to a high risk of choroidal effusions after any intraocular surgery. Awadalla et al. (2014) named angle-closure glaucoma as one of the main complications. Yu et al. (2009) described simple microphthalmia, a structurally normal but small eye globe, as an uncommon congenital or developmental ocular anomaly that is usually bilateral, with a short axis and hyperopia of +7.00 to +13.00 diopters. Nanophthalmos-4 is the autosomal dominant form caused by mutation in TMEM98, which Awadalla et al. (2014) reported as the first gene identified to cause autosomal dominant nanophthalmos.

paragraphs.text: Khorram et al. (2015) noted that nanophthalmos is genetically heterogeneous and that both autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive forms have been reported. Several cases of recessive nanophthalmos have been attributed to mutations in the MFRP gene.

checks.claim: Nanophthalmos is genetically heterogeneous.
checks.evidence_quote: Nanophthalmos has a strong genetic basis, and autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive forms of inheritance have been reported. Mutations in the membrane-type frizzled-related protein (MFRP, OMIM 606227) have been detected in a large recessive nanophthalmos pedigree.
checks.explanation: The paper never uses the word 'heterogeneous'. It does describe different inheritance modes and different genes (MFRP and TMEM98), which implies heterogeneity.

paragraphs.text: Awadalla et al. (2014) studied one large white family (NNO-SA1) with autosomal dominant nanophthalmos. Exome sequencing found a single novel missense variant within the linkage region. The variant lay in exon 8 of the transmembrane-98 (TMEM98) gene: a c.577G-C change that results in an ala193-to-pro (A193P) substitution. The variant segregated with the disease in the family.
